chapter_theme: One song at Tirutturutti (திருத்துருத்தி): the poet confesses to courtesans who are never satisfied with any sum and to the disease that follows, and recalls that Murugan called him, gave him the experience of release and told him to recite the Thiruppugazh.

846.reading: The poet describes the courtesans, heavy-breasted and thread-waisted, who loosen their garments and bewitch with spear eyes, then turn their glance against the men who trusted them, say that even thousands upon thousands of gold coins poured on their breasts are not enough, and cast men off; he calls himself a vain man whom a great disease has crippled and shamed and asks for the lightning-bright feet. The praise names Murugan who called him, a dog, as one taking refuge, gave him the experience of release and bade him recite the Thiruppugazh, the child who gave a poem in triple Tamil to the teacher who burned the three cities, and Valli's lover at Tirutturutti.
846.nuance: அழைத்து முத்தியதாம் அநுபூதி என் அருள் திருப்புகழ் ஓதுக வேல் மயில் அருள்வோனே: the poet's own call, in which Murugan names the Thiruppugazh, appears here in the praise, as in 2. The line on the teacher (தேசிகர்) of the three cities and the poem in triple Tamil may refer to Siva or to a saint, and the reading is tentative. மகாபிணி after the courtesans is a disease caught from them.

links.note: Both recall the moment Murugan told the poet to sing the Thiruppugazh; 846 adds that he called him as one taking refuge and gave him the experience of release first.
The Naladiyar says the courtesan's love ends when the man's money ends; 846 goes further, that no amount, thousands of thousands of gold coins, ever satisfies her.
